name: Gabapentin (Neurontin)
summary: Gabapentin is a calming, nerve-signal “dimmer switch” that’s sometimes used in psychiatry for anxiety, sleep problems, and alcohol-related symptoms—especially when first-line options don’t fit. It can be sedating, needs kidney-based dosing, and can be risky with opioids or other downers.
description: Gabapentin is best known as a seizure and nerve pain medication, but in real-world psychiatry it shows up as an off-label option for anxiety (GAD, panic, social anxiety), sleep disruption, and alcohol withdrawal/alcohol use disorder—usually as an adjunct or backup plan. It can cause dizziness, drowsiness, and brain-fog, and in higher-risk patients (older adults, lung disease, or when combined with opioids/benzodiazepines/alcohol) it can cause dangerous sedation and breathing problems. It’s cleared by the kidneys, so dosing has to match renal function. Don’t swap it with gabapentin enacarbil products—they’re not equivalent.
patient_summary: Gabapentin can take the edge off anxiety, help sleep settle, and sometimes smooth alcohol withdrawal symptoms—especially when other meds aren’t an option. The tradeoff: it can make you sleepy, dizzy, and foggy, and it becomes dangerous when mixed with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives. If you have kidney problems, the dose has to be adjusted. Don’t stop suddenly after regular use—taper down.

metadata.controlled_substance: Not federally scheduled (US); controlled in some states and settings

primary_indications: Alcohol Use Disorder, Moderate to Severe (off-label)
Sleep Disruption with Nighttime Symptoms (off-label use patterns)

linked_conditions.context: Used in some protocols for mild-to-moderate withdrawal or as an alternative/adjunct when benzodiazepines aren’t appropriate. Dosing is flexible and often guided by withdrawal severity (eg, CIWA scores) and setting (inpatient vs ambulatory).

Sometimes used as an alternative agent when first-line AUD meds can’t be used. It may reduce withdrawal-driven cravings/anxiety in some patients, but misuse risk matters—screen for addiction risk and monitor closely.
Used as a short-term add-on for symptom relief while first-line treatments (therapy/SSRIs/SNRIs) ramp up, or as longer-term augmentation when response is partial.
Sometimes used as augmentation for SSRIs/SNRIs when patients need faster symptom relief or only get partial benefit from antidepressants alone.
Reserved for people who don’t tolerate or respond to preferred options. Typically titrated slowly to balance anxiety relief with sedation and dizziness.

Often used when sleep problems are tightly linked to nighttime symptoms (restlessness, hot flashes, pain-arousal patterns, withdrawal-related insomnia). Dosing is usually bedtime-weighted to use the sedating effect intentionally.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to gabapentin or any component of the formulation

efficacy_response.patient_text: Gabapentin’s psychiatric uses are mostly off-label and depend heavily on the situation (withdrawal severity, sleep pattern, comorbid anxiety, and whether it’s being used alone or as an add-on). In practice, the goal is functional improvement—less withdrawal intensity, fewer nighttime awakenings, and less “wired” anxiety—without trading it for heavy sedation or dizziness.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Variable and saturable (dose-dependent); absorbed in proximal small bowel by L-amino transport system
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: Decreases as total daily dose increases due to saturable absorption (eg, ~60% at 900 mg/day; ~33% at 3,600 mg/day)
pharmacokinetics.onset: Varied; clinical calming/sedation can be noticed within hours, but steady benefit for chronic symptoms often takes days to weeks as the dose is titrated
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: Immediate release: 2 to 4 hours (adults); Extended release: ~8 hours
pharmacokinetics.half_life: 5 to 7 hours in adults with normal renal function (prolonged with renal impairment)
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Typically requires divided dosing; when dosed TID, avoid >12 hours between doses
pharmacokinetics.duration_XR: Designed for once-daily dosing (taken with evening meal); not interchangeable with IR products
pharmacokinetics.excretion: Renal excretion as unchanged drug; clearance proportional to creatinine clearance
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Immediate release: no significant effect; Extended release: food increases absorption—take ER with the evening meal

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: In psychiatry, gabapentin is an off-label option for anxiety, sleep disruption, and alcohol-related symptoms—usually as a backup plan or add-on when first-line treatments aren’t possible or aren’t enough. It’s not a first-line anxiety med, and it’s not “benzo-lite.” It can help some people, but it can also make you foggy, wobbly, or overly sedated—especially if you mix it with other downers.
items: {link:condition:generalized-anxiety-disorder:Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD)} (off-label): Used as short-term symptom relief while SSRIs/SNRIs/therapy ramp up, or augmentation when response is partial
{link:condition:panic-disorder:Panic Disorder} (off-label, augmentation): Sometimes added when antidepressants aren’t fully controlling panic and faster relief is needed
{link:condition:social-anxiety-disorder:Social Anxiety Disorder} (off-label): Reserved for people who don’t tolerate or respond to preferred agents
{link:condition:alcohol-withdrawal:Alcohol Withdrawal} (off-label): Used in some regimens for mild-to-moderate withdrawal or as an alternative/adjunct in select cases
{link:condition:alcohol-use-disorder:Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD)} (off-label): Sometimes used as an alternative agent when first-line AUD meds can’t be used
{link:condition:insomnia:Sleep disruption} (off-label patterns): Especially when symptoms are worse at night (restlessness, hot flashes, withdrawal insomnia, sleep fragmentation)
off_label: Nighttime symptom clusters where sedation is a feature, not a side effect (sleep disturbance, nighttime restlessness)
Adjunctive calming in select patients when other options are limited (must assess misuse risk carefully)

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: Gabapentin can feel subtle for some people and dramatic for others. Here’s the real-world vibe patients describe most often:

quotes: It didn’t knock out my anxiety instantly—more like it turned the intensity down over a few days.
My body felt less keyed up. I wasn’t white-knuckling the day as much.
It took the edge off without making me feel emotionally numb.

items.category: Sleep help (when nighttime is the problem)
quotes: My brain stopped doing the 2 a.m. doom-scroll in my head.
I still woke up, but I could fall back asleep instead of spiraling.
It made me sleepy in a way that felt like ‘normal sleepy,’ not drugged.
items.note: Bedtime-weighted dosing is common when sleep is the target.

quotes: I felt wobbly, like I had sea legs.
My brain felt slower—fine for bedtime, not great for meetings.
I was tired and spacey until my dose stabilized.
items.note: Dizziness and drowsiness are dose-related and more likely during titration.

quotes: It took the shakiness and wired feeling down a notch.
It helped with the anxiety part of withdrawal more than the whole thing.
When cravings spiked, it gave me a little buffer—but I still needed a plan.
items.note: Withdrawal regimens vary by severity and setting; this is not a one-size-fits-all med.

quotes: It was helpful, but I noticed I started wanting extra on bad days.
I had to be honest with myself about why I was reaching for it.
My doctor asked the right questions about addiction history—and that mattered.
items.note: Gabapentin can be misused, especially in people with substance use disorders. Screening and monitoring aren’t optional.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Gabapentin isn’t usually an instant switch-flip like a benzodiazepine. It’s more of a dose-and-time medication: you feel the sedating effect early, but the fuller benefit for anxiety, sleep stabilization, or withdrawal support often shows up as the dose is titrated.
key_points: First-dose effects: Drowsiness/dizziness can show up quickly (often the reason many clinicians start the first dose at bedtime)
Peak blood levels: Immediate-release peaks in ~2–4 hours; extended-release peaks later (~8 hours)
Daily rhythm: IR often needs divided doses; if taking it three times daily, avoid gaps longer than 12 hours
Half-life: ~5–7 hours in adults with normal kidneys (can get much longer with kidney impairment)
Extended-release: Designed for once-daily dosing and should be taken with the evening meal

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Gabapentin’s psychiatric use is situation-dependent. When it helps, patients often describe less physical anxiety, fewer nighttime awakenings, and smoother withdrawal-related symptoms. The biggest limiter is tolerability (dizziness, sedation, cognitive slowing) and safety in higher-risk groups (older adults, respiratory disease, and anyone combining it with opioids or other sedatives).
sections.clinical_details: In psychiatric practice, gabapentin is typically positioned as (1) an alternative or adjunct for anxiety disorders when preferred agents aren’t tolerated or are only partially effective, (2) a bedtime-weighted option when sleep disruption is prominent, and (3) a protocol-based option in select alcohol withdrawal/AUD scenarios. Response is usually judged by functional outcomes (sleep continuity, reduced panic frequency/intensity, reduced withdrawal severity) rather than a single standardized metric.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Biggest safety issue: dangerous sedation and breathing suppression when combined with opioids, alcohol, or other CNS depressants—especially in older adults or people with lung disease.
other: CNS and respiratory depression can occur; risk increases with opioids and other sedatives and in patients with underlying respiratory impairment or older age
Suicidal thoughts/behavior risk has been reported with antiseizure medications; monitor mood, agitation, and new behavioral changes—especially in the first weeks
Do not substitute gabapentin products interchangeably: immediate-release, extended-release (eg, Gralise), and gabapentin enacarbil are not equivalent
Renal impairment requires dose adjustment; accumulation increases sedation, confusion, and falls
Hypersensitivity reactions can occur, including angioedema/anaphylaxis and severe skin reactions (rare but serious)
Use caution in myasthenia gravis (may worsen symptoms)
Misuse/dependence can occur, especially in patients with a history of substance misuse
patient_counseling: If you take opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol, sedating antihistamines, or sleep meds, tell your prescriber—mixing sedatives can be dangerous.
Start low and go slow, especially if you have COPD, sleep apnea, or other respiratory disease.
If you feel excessively sleepy, confused, or your breathing feels slow/shallow, treat that like a real warning sign—don’t just ‘push through.’
Don’t switch formulations on your own. Gralise is not the same as regular gabapentin, and gabapentin enacarbil is a different product with different pharmacokinetics.
If you’ve had addiction issues before, say it out loud. This med can be misused, and the safest plan is an honest plan.
Don’t stop suddenly after regular use—taper down with your clinician.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: dizziness, drowsiness, fatigue, and coordination problems. In psychiatry, the line between “helpful sedation” and “too foggy to function” is the main balancing act.
plain_language_list: Brain fog: slower thinking, memory or concentration problems
Mood/behavior changes (more reported in kids, but can occur in adults)

common.incidence: Common (often reported in adults; frequency varies by study and formulation)
common.patient_note: This is the classic early side effect. People describe feeling wobbly or off-balance, especially during the first week or after dose increases. Dose changes at night and slower titration can help.

common.incidence: Common (often reported in adults and adolescents)
common.patient_note: Sedation can be the point (if we’re targeting sleep) or the problem (if you’re trying to function during the day). If you feel overly sedated, the dose may be too high, the titration too fast, or another sedating medication may be stacking the effect.

common.incidence: Reported in some studies (can be more noticeable at higher doses)
common.patient_note: This is the ‘I’m not safe on stairs’ side effect. It matters more in older adults and anyone with a fall history. If you feel unsteady, don’t ignore it.

common.incidence: Reported (varies by dose and individual sensitivity)
common.patient_note: Some people feel slower, spacey, or less sharp. In psychiatry, this can be a deal-breaker if the med helps anxiety but costs too much cognition.
Swelling in feet/legs can happen. Let your clinician know—especially if it’s new, worsening, or you have heart/kidney issues.
Not everyone gains weight, but it’s common enough to be worth tracking—especially if the medication becomes long-term.

serious: Respiratory depression: life-threatening sedation/breathing suppression, especially with opioids or in patients with respiratory disease or older age
Severe hypersensitivity: angioedema/anaphylaxis (swelling of lips/tongue/throat, trouble breathing) — emergency
Severe skin reactions (rare): Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis/DRESS — urgent medical evaluation
Suicidal thoughts/behavior: monitor closely, especially early in treatment or during dose changes
Neuropsychiatric effects: agitation, behavioral changes, disinhibition (more reported in pediatrics but can occur in adults, especially vulnerable brains)
Withdrawal syndrome after abrupt stopping: confusion, irritability, sweating, tachycardia, insomnia, rebound anxiety; taper is safer

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Gabapentin isn’t heavily metabolized, so it doesn’t have the classic liver-enzyme interaction profile—but it absolutely can interact in the real world through additive sedation and respiratory suppression.

items.risk: Major: additive CNS depression and life-threatening respiratory depression, especially in older adults or people with respiratory impairment.
items.action: Avoid the combo when possible. If it’s necessary, use the lowest doses, titrate slowly, and monitor closely for oversedation, confusion, and breathing problems.

items.risk: Additive sedation and impaired coordination; higher overdose-like risk when stacked with other CNS depressants.
items.action: Best practice: avoid alcohol while titrating and avoid heavy drinking while on gabapentin—especially if there’s any opioid/benzo exposure or respiratory risk.

items.with: Benzodiazepines, sleep meds, sedating antihistamines, muscle relaxants
items.risk: Sedation stacking: dizziness, falls, confusion, impaired driving, respiratory suppression in high-risk patients.
items.action: Treat this as a dose-stacking problem. Reduce doses, separate timing when possible, and reassess whether you need both.

items.with: Formulation swaps (IR vs ER vs gabapentin enacarbil)
items.risk: Medication errors and unexpected blood-level patterns due to different pharmacokinetic profiles and indications.
items.action: Do not substitute products as if they’re the same medication. Confirm formulation and instructions at every refill.

items.risk: Extended-release absorption is increased with food; taking it without food can change exposure.
items.action: Take ER with the evening meal, consistently.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: If you’ve been taking gabapentin regularly, don’t stop suddenly. Even though it’s not a benzodiazepine, abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal symptoms (confusion, irritability, sweating, fast heart rate), rebound insomnia, and rebound anxiety. Standard guidance is to taper gradually over at least 1 week, and longer tapers are often more comfortable after chronic use or higher doses.
key_points: Minimum taper window: ≥1 week for most chronic use (longer is often better if dose is high or symptoms rebound easily)
Common rebound/withdrawal symptoms: insomnia, anxiety, irritability, sweating, tachycardia, restlessness, nausea
Higher-risk situations: older adults, renal impairment (accumulation), concurrent sedatives, and patients using gabapentin in alcohol-related protocols
If you’re using it for alcohol withdrawal or AUD: tapering plans depend on the protocol—don’t freestyle this without clinical guidance
If significant withdrawal symptoms appear: slow the taper, stabilize, and step down more gradually

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Psychiatric dosing with gabapentin is almost always off-label and depends on the target: anxiety relief, sleep stabilization, or alcohol-related symptoms. The main rules: start low, titrate slowly, and adjust for kidney function. If a patient has respiratory disease or is on other sedatives, the safest move is the lowest possible starting dose with slow escalation.

adult.aud_initial: Immediate release: 300 mg PO once daily; increase by 300 mg every 1 to 2 days based on response and tolerability
adult.aud_target: Immediate release: Target 600 mg PO three times daily (1,800 mg/day); reassess if goals aren’t met within 4 to 6 months
adult.withdrawal_ciwascore_lt10: Immediate release: Day 1: 300 mg PO every 6 hours; Day 2: 300 mg PO every 8 hours; Day 3: 300 mg PO every 12 hours; Day 4: 300 mg PO at night. Plus: one additional 300 mg PO PRN per day for breakthrough symptoms
adult.withdrawal_ciwascore_10_18: Immediate release: Days 1–3: 300–400 mg PO three times daily; Day 4: 300–400 mg PO twice daily, then stop. Breakthrough option: 100 mg single doses up to 3 times daily, plus a 300 mg evening dose reserved for night symptoms
adult.gad_initial: Immediate release: 300 mg/day PO; in side-effect-sensitive patients, consider 100 mg/day to start
adult.gad_titration: Increase gradually based on response and tolerability (commonly in 100–300 mg/day steps) to divided dosing 2 to 3 times daily
adult.gad_max: Up to 2,400 mg/day PO in 2 to 3 divided doses (off-label guidance)
adult.panic_initial: Immediate release: 200 mg PO three times daily (off-label, augmentation)
adult.panic_titration: Increase by 600 to 900 mg/day at weekly intervals based on response and tolerability
adult.social_anxiety_initial: Immediate release: 300 mg PO twice daily; in higher-risk respiratory disease, some experts start as low as 100 mg PO three times daily
adult.social_anxiety_titration: Increase by no more than 300 mg/day based on response and tolerability, divided into 3 daily doses as dose rises
adult.social_anxiety_max: 3,600 mg/day PO in 3 divided doses (off-label guidance)
adult.sleep_initial: Immediate release: 100–300 mg PO at bedtime (used when sleep disruption is prominent, including nighttime symptoms)
adult.sleep_titration: Increase gradually every 1 to 4 weeks based on response and tolerability; often keep dosing bedtime-weighted if sedation is helpful
adult.sleep_max: Common target ranges vary by condition; off-label patterns may reach 1,200–2,400 mg/day in divided doses when treating broader symptom clusters (balance against daytime fog and dizziness)
adult.rls_initial: Immediate release: 100–300 mg PO once daily about 2 hours before bedtime
adult.rls_titration: Increase every 1 to 2 weeks until symptom relief (maintenance commonly 300 mg/day to 1,800 mg/day; when ≥600 mg/day, one-third midday and two-thirds evening is one suggested split)

sections.simple_explanation: Immediate-release gabapentin can be used in divided doses for daytime anxiety and evening sleep support. Extended-release gabapentin (Gralise) is taken once daily with the evening meal and isn’t interchangeable with immediate-release. For alcohol withdrawal protocols, dosing is often schedule-based and tied to symptom severity rather than a single fixed dose.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Gabapentin needs extra thought in pregnancy, breastfeeding, older adults, and anyone with kidney or respiratory disease. In psychiatry, the risk/benefit decision is very indication-specific (withdrawal stabilization vs chronic anxiety vs sleep).
sections.pregnancy: Evaluate pregnancy status prior to use when clinically relevant. Gabapentin crosses the placenta. In epilepsy populations, gabapentin monotherapy has been associated with lower risks of major congenital malformations compared with some other antiseizure medications, but data are not enough to fully define neurodevelopmental risk. When gabapentin is used near delivery in combination with opioids for extended periods, neonatal withdrawal risk may increase. For alcohol use disorder in pregnancy, pharmacologic agents are generally avoided unless needed for acute withdrawal or a coexisting disorder; other agents may be preferred when treatment is needed.
sections.lactation: Gabapentin is present in breast milk. Limited human data suggest relative infant doses in the low single digits (%) with no reported adverse events in small case series, but the dataset is small. If breastfeeding during therapy, monitor the infant for sedation, poor feeding, appropriate weight gain, and normal development. Consider checking infant serum concentrations if toxicity symptoms appear.
sections.geriatrics: Initiate at the lowest dose and titrate slowly. Older adults are more vulnerable to dizziness, sedation, confusion, and falls—especially with other sedatives or kidney impairment. If the patient has recurrent falls or significant gait instability, the risk may outweigh benefit.
sections.hepatic: Gabapentin is not hepatically metabolized. In cirrhosis with Child-Turcotte-Pugh class B/C before starting, some recommendations suggest an initial dose ≤300 mg/day in 1 to 3 divided doses and titrate carefully as tolerated. Use extra caution in hepatic encephalopathy risk states and when other CNS depressants are present.
sections.renal: Renal function drives dosing. Dose reduction is required in reduced creatinine clearance to prevent accumulation (sedation, confusion, falls). Immediate-release maintenance maximums by CrCl are commonly capped at: >79 mL/min: up to 3,600 mg/day; 50–79 mL/min: not to exceed 1,800 mg/day; 30–49 mL/min: ~50% reduction (max ~900 mg/day); 15–29 mL/min: ~75% reduction (max ~600 mg/day); <15 mL/min: ~90% reduction (max ~300 mg/day). Hemodialysis requires post-dialysis dosing; extended-release products are generally not recommended in significant renal impairment.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Sedation and dizziness: especially during initiation and dose increases; assess fall risk and driving safety
Respiratory depression risk: monitor closely in older adults, patients with underlying respiratory impairment, and anyone on opioids or other sedatives
Mood and suicidality: monitor for new/worsening depression, suicidal thoughts, agitation, irritability, or behavioral changes—particularly in the first 1 to 12 weeks
Cognitive side effects: brain fog, slowed thinking, confusion (higher risk with renal impairment or medication stacking)
Misuse risk: screen for substance use disorder history (alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, stimulants, cannabis) and monitor for escalating use or non-prescribed patterns
Renal function: periodic creatinine clearance/renal function checks, especially in older adults or anyone with known kidney disease
Alcohol withdrawal protocols: if using for withdrawal, monitor symptom trajectory (eg, CIWA-style monitoring when applicable), breakthrough symptoms, and safety in the chosen setting
Edema and weight: watch for peripheral edema and weight gain if used longer-term

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Gabapentin comes in immediate-release and extended-release forms. These are not interchangeable, and the dosing instructions are different.
items: Extended-release tablets (Gralise): 300 mg, 450 mg, 600 mg, 750 mg, 900 mg (take with evening meal; swallow whole)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Gabapentin is structurally related to GABA, but it doesn’t bind to GABA-A or GABA-B receptors and doesn’t directly boost GABA the way benzodiazepines do. Its main action is binding to the alpha-2-delta-1 subunit of certain voltage-gated calcium channels in the brain, which can reduce release of excitatory neurotransmitters. Clinically, that can translate into less “overfiring” in certain circuits—showing up as calming, less restlessness, and sometimes better sleep continuity.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: In psychiatry, gabapentin is usually not a first-line medication for anxiety disorders or insomnia. It’s more of a targeted tool: useful when (1) anxiety is strongly physical and sedation is acceptable, (2) sleep disruption is a major driver of distress and nighttime dosing is a good fit, or (3) alcohol-related symptoms require an alternative/adjunct strategy. The safety conversation matters: renal dosing, fall risk, respiratory risk with sedative stacking, and misuse potential—especially in patients with substance use histories.

seo.title: Gabapentin (Neurontin): Anxiety, Sleep, Alcohol Withdrawal Uses, Dosing, Side Effects
seo.description: Gabapentin (Neurontin/Gralise): psychiatry-focused guide to off-label uses for anxiety, panic, social anxiety, sleep disruption, and alcohol withdrawal/AUD—plus dosing patterns, side effects, safety warnings, interactions, and tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Not officially. For anxiety, gabapentin is an off-label option—usually a backup plan or add-on when first-line treatments (therapy, SSRIs/SNRIs) aren’t possible or aren’t enough. When it helps, it often targets the physical “wired” feeling of anxiety, but sedation and dizziness can limit use.

faqs.q: How fast does gabapentin work for anxiety or sleep?
faqs.a: The sedating effect can show up quickly (often within hours), which is why many people take the first dose at bedtime. For anxiety relief and sleep stabilization, the fuller benefit often shows up over days to weeks as the dose is titrated to a tolerable and effective range.

faqs.q: Can gabapentin help with alcohol withdrawal?
faqs.a: It can be used in some off-label withdrawal regimens, especially for mild-to-moderate scenarios or as an alternative/adjunct when benzodiazepines aren’t appropriate. Dosing is usually protocol-based and depends on withdrawal severity and treatment setting. It’s not a DIY medication for withdrawal—safety monitoring matters.

faqs.q: Can gabapentin be misused or addictive?
faqs.a: Yes, it can be misused, especially in people with a history of substance use disorders. That doesn’t mean everyone will misuse it, but it does mean prescribers should screen for risk and monitor for dose escalation, early refills, or using it for reasons outside the plan.

faqs.q: What’s the biggest safety risk with gabapentin?
faqs.a: Sedation and breathing suppression when it’s combined with opioids or other CNS depressants—especially in older adults or people with respiratory disease. If someone is very sleepy, confused, or breathing seems slow/shallow, that’s a serious warning sign.

faqs.q: Do I need dose changes if I have kidney disease?
faqs.a: Yes. Gabapentin is cleared by the kidneys, so impaired renal function can cause the medication to build up and increase side effects like sedation, confusion, and falls. Dosing should be adjusted based on creatinine clearance, and extended-release products may not be recommended in more severe renal impairment.

faqs.q: Is Gralise the same as Neurontin?
faqs.a: No. Gralise is an extended-release gabapentin product with different dosing instructions (taken with the evening meal) and it’s not interchangeable with immediate-release gabapentin. Also, gabapentin enacarbil products are not the same as gabapentin.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol on gabapentin?
faqs.a: Mixing gabapentin and alcohol can increase dizziness, sedation, impaired coordination, and risky decision-making—especially if there are other sedatives involved. If gabapentin is being used for alcohol-related symptoms, drinking on top of it also undermines the whole treatment goal.

faqs.q: Do I need to taper gabapentin?
faqs.a: If you’ve been taking it regularly, yes—tapering is safer than stopping suddenly. Abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal-type symptoms like insomnia, irritability, sweating, fast heart rate, confusion, and rebound anxiety. A gradual taper over at least a week is typical, and longer tapers can be more comfortable after chronic use.

faqs.q: Why do some people feel foggy or dizzy on gabapentin?
faqs.a: Those are common dose-related CNS side effects. They’re more likely during titration, at higher doses, in older adults, and when gabapentin is combined with other sedatives—or when the dose isn’t adjusted for kidney function.

faqs.q: Is gabapentin safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: It depends on the reason for use and the alternatives. Gabapentin crosses the placenta, and pregnancy data are more developed in epilepsy populations than in psychiatric off-label use. In breastfeeding, gabapentin is present in milk; limited data suggest relatively low infant exposure, but monitoring for infant sedation and feeding issues is important. These decisions should be individualized with careful risk/benefit planning.
